job.country_name: Congo, The Democratic Republic of the

reconnaissance_summary.censorship_and_self_censorship: Criticism was possible through international organizations, NGOs, press-freedom groups, research institutes, local media, humanitarian assessments, and parliamentary monitors, but intimidation, detention, self-censorship, protest restrictions, and restricted military-site access constrained reporting.
chapter_specific_biases: 1B: treaty and diplomatic records establish policy and legal status but do not verify internal nuclear safety or technical oversight.
2B: eastern conflict incidents and accessible severe events may be overrepresented; state-of-siege attribution is clearer than attribution of every outcome.
3B: conflict-area, detention, and media evidence is incomplete nationally; accountability counts do not prove effective remedy.
4B: country indices and formal electoral procedures do not establish fairness, direct intervention, campaign-finance integrity, or transfer compliance.
5B: donor-supported programs, retrospective audits, external shocks, and weak distributional data complicate attribution.
6B: education, humanitarian, and vaccination evidence is concentrated in donor and partner reporting; health, reach, and durability remain weakly verified.
7B: anti-corruption actions and associate-related cases do not establish personal enrichment, family benefit, knowledge, deception, retaliation, or obstruction.
8B: operationalization evidence exceeds durable outcome evidence; donor reporting, shocks, and incomplete peace-process implementation constrain attribution.
reconnaissance_summary.complaint_volume_interpretation: Reported complaints and incidents are not population denominators. Visible opposition, media, humanitarian, and conflict cases may be overrepresented while self-censorship and inaccessible areas suppress complaints.
reconnaissance_summary.criticism_possible: Criticism was possible through international organizations, independent NGOs, press-freedom organizations, research institutes, local media, humanitarian assessments, and parliamentary monitors; access and safety constraints limited criticism in conflict and detention settings.
reconnaissance_summary.duplicate_event_risk: High. Shared U.S. report-family units, overlapping state-of-siege incidents, diplomacy records, and donor reporting were retained only where claims were materially distinct.
reconnaissance_summary.inherited_conditions_shocks_and_authorit: The DRC entered 2022 with severe conflict, poverty, weak institutions, low service baselines, and limited practical civilian control. Tshisekedi had formal authority over national policy, appointments, APLC, emergency powers, security-sector direction, and peace-process participation. External shocks included the Ukraine war, food and energy inflation, mining-market changes, COVID-19, displacement, and conflict.
reconnaissance_summary.official_statistics_reliability: Structured indicators and humanitarian statistics are useful for country-year exposure and outcomes but do not establish ruler-specific responsibility. Official claims were marked unverified or non-independent where applicable.
reconnaissance_summary.relevant_denominators: Available denominators include conflict events and fatalities, one-sided violence, military expenditure, press-freedom violations, IPC populations, people in need, IDPs, health zones, vaccination reach, and beneficiaries. Exposure-adjusted national denominators remain incomplete.
reconnaissance_summary.safe_reporting_channels: Channels included international organizations, UN mechanisms, humanitarian agencies, NGOs, press-freedom groups, local media, research institutes, parliamentary monitors, and formal treaty/electoral records. Intimidation, detention, self-censorship, and restricted military-site access made safety and completeness uneven.
reconnaissance_summary.source_concentration: Evidence is strongest in intergovernmental, human-rights, donor, humanitarian, and official records. World Bank/UNICEF material is concentrated in 5B, 6B, and 8B; U.S. reporting in 2B and 3B; personal-integrity evidence remains sparse and attribution-heavy.

resource_index.claim: Human Rights Watch documented suppression of peaceful critics, lethal protest response, arbitrary detention, and broad martial-law restrictions in North Kivu and Ituri.
resource_index.locator: Report sections on martial-law powers, protests, detention, and military courts

resource_index.claim: The U.S. 2022 report records killings, torture, disappearances, abusive detention, limited civilian control, and some prosecutions and training.
resource_index.locator: 2022 Country Reports on Human Rights Practices, executive summary and sections on killings, detention, expression, and accountability

resource_index.claim: OHCHR and MONUSCO found torture concentrated in conflict areas and impunity widespread, while documenting legal reform and monitoring efforts.
resource_index.locator: PDF sections on torture patterns, conflict areas, impunity, legal reform, and monitoring

resource_index.claim: Journalist in Danger recorded 124 press-freedom violations in 2022, including one death and two abductions.
resource_index.locator: French-language report summary paragraphs reporting the 2022 JED count

resource_index.claim: Amnesty’s 2022 review records killings and abuses by Congolese forces in western DRC, three soldiers convicted for killing civilians, and 28 more awaiting trial.
CPJ documented two journalists detained without charge for five months after covering a protest involving opposition provincial deputies, with conflicting procedural explanations.

After one year of state of siege, military authorities had assumed civil powers without achieving the stated security objective and used exceptional powers against expression, assembly, and justice rights.
Actualité.cd reported that 71 soldiers and 20 police officers were convicted for rights-related offenses during 2022 and transitional-justice consultations reached 22,178 people in eight provinces.
Amnesty reported repeated state-of-siege extensions, military-court use for civilians, detention of critics, and increased civilian deaths despite the protection rationale.
resource_index.locator: Briefing opening summary and sections on extensions, military courts, detention, and civilian deaths

resource_index.claim: Congo Research Group summarized UN findings on RDF support for M23, M23 attacks on civilians, and FARDC cooperation with local armed groups.
The IMF records APLC involvement in 36 cases, including 26 alleged embezzlement cases, and government validation of an anti-corruption strategy.
HRW reported widespread violence by M23, other armed groups, and sometimes government soldiers; UN evidence indicated RDF personnel in M23 camps, while Rwanda denied support.
resource_index.locator: Report paragraphs on M23 resurgence, civilian attacks, and RDF evidence
